title: 1 Introduction
summary: This capstone implements secure container delivery from GitHub to AWS and keeps an independent local Docker demonstration available. The completed release passes preventive security gates, cryptographic verification and ECS health checks. Evidence is recorded against a specific source commit and image digest, rather than inferred from the presence of cloud resources.

blocks.text: A container can be deployable while its source, dependencies or delivery credentials remain unsafe. A reproducible security engineering workflow must examine the source, infrastructure, image and deployment decision together. This project demonstrates those checks with a deliberately small application so the delivery controls can be reviewed clearly.

The original AWS CodePipeline design reached its source stage, but CodeBuild could not start because applied account and regional concurrency was zero. AdministratorAccess did not override the service quota. The final architecture moves CI computation to GitHub Actions while ECR, ECS, Falco and AWS monitoring remain on AWS. The exact account restriction was observed; its underlying account-policy reason was not established.

The report covers requirements, use cases, artifact modeling, data flows, threats, attack paths, operational interfaces, implementation changes, tests and verified deployment. It documents a single-account educational deployment in Mumbai and a localhost-only Docker app in D:\aws.

The application exposes JSON at / and /health. It has no authentication system, database, user-upload feature or interactive command execution. The engineering scope is the secure delivery and runtime observation of this service. Production availability, multi-account governance and a full enterprise security audit are outside this baseline.

blocks.text: A manifest is not proof of trust by itself. The verifier rejects malformed identities, a different repository, a different source commit or a signature that does not match the trusted key. ECS receives the digest, avoiding tag-resolution ambiguity.

title: 6 Threat Modeling
summary: The threat model is a design analysis of this implementation. It distinguishes controls verified in tests from residual trust in administrators and reviewed main-branch code. A threat scenario is not a claim that the account was compromised.

rows: Controls what code is scanned and released

blocks.text: The app uses a whitelist of two GET paths and never maps request paths to filesystem reads or commands. JSON log encoding reduces the risk of forged plain-text log entries. Runtime application privileges are minimized independently from the Falco sensor. These controls reduce the relevant surface; they do not establish the absence of every vulnerability in Python, Docker, the kernel or CI tools.

The Checkov control set is selected, Semgrep uses three project rules, and scanner results depend on supported formats and database state. Tool transitive dependencies are not fully hash-locked. A future HIGH/CRITICAL finding can legitimately fail a release even when this dated run passed.

blocks.text: An accepted Cosign signature establishes integrity relative to the trusted signing key. It does not prove independent build provenance, source safety or that every reviewer approved the change. Keyed private signing deliberately omits public transparency-log verification. Future hardening should strengthen reviewer controls and provenance without weakening the current digest verifier.

blocks.text: The supplied screenshot contains runtime deprecation warnings from older action versions. The final release uses the updated Node 24 pins. Exact source and digest come from the downloaded final release/deployment artifacts and are checked against current ECS configuration.

A harmless shell execution inside the AWS application produced an actual Falco Warning event. The event includes the application container identity and is stored in CloudWatch. Sensor inspection confirms active status, no OOM and zero restarts at the check. This establishes demonstrated detection for the chosen probe, not comprehensive coverage of all runtime attacks.

Falco detection differs from application isolation. The sensor needs host capabilities and Docker-socket access; the app does not receive them. CloudTrail Event History provides management API audit lookup, while a durable trail is future work. GitHub CI logs are retained in GitHub and are not described as native CodePipeline events.

blocks.text: The project demonstrates a complete scan, build, sign, verify and deploy chain using GitHub Actions and AWS runtime services. CodeBuild capacity no longer blocks this active path. The verified AWS task runs a content-addressed image under constrained application permissions, Falco produces an observed runtime warning, and the local hardened service remains available independently.

The evidence supports this educational baseline. Selected scanner coverage, private keyed signing, short retention, trusted administrators and a single small host remain explicit limits. Further production work should strengthen governance, provenance, retained audit and availability while preserving the existing fail-closed deployment checks.
